Keep all fuels and solvents in clearly labelled, child-resistant containers, locked away from children.
Educate families on the danger of hydrocarbon ingestion and harmful first-aid practices (such as inducing vomiting).
Promote safer cooking and lighting options where possible, and proper ventilation when using fuels indoors.
references: WHO and paediatric toxicology resources – Hydrocarbon and kerosene poisoning in children.
MSD Manual and clinical guidelines – Hydrocarbon poisoning, aspiration pneumonitis and management.
International First Aid and Red Cross training materials – Poisoning and specific hydrocarbon exposures.
Regional studies from low- and middle-income countries where kerosene use in homes is common.

description: Injury caused by contact with household electrical current (typically 110–240V), which may cause burns, muscle contractions, heart rhythm disturbances, or loss of consciousness.
causes: Touching exposed wires or damaged electrical cables
Using electrical devices with wet hands
Faulty heaters, water boilers, or washing machines
Short circuits in old or poorly maintained installations
risk_factors: Metal jewelry or tools during electrical work

common: Pain or burning at entry/exit points

first_aid_steps: Ensure the scene is safe and disconnect power before touching the person.
Check responsiveness, airway, and breathing.
If unconscious and not breathing, begin CPR and call emergency services.
Cool minor burns with clean running water for 20 minutes.
Cover burns with a sterile non-stick dressing.
Monitor for chest pain, palpitations, confusion, or weakness.
what_not_to_do: Do not touch the person while the power is still on.
Do not apply ice directly to burns.
Do not use butter, oil, or toothpaste on burns.
Do not assume the person is fine because injuries are not visible.
when_to_call_emergency: Loss of consciousness at any moment.
Chest pain, palpitations, or irregular heartbeat.
Burns larger than a coin or involving the face/hands/genitals.
Difficulty breathing or persistent confusion.
prevention: Use grounded plugs and avoid overloading outlets.
Keep electrical devices away from water.
Repair damaged cables immediately.
Install outlet covers in homes with children.
references: WHO–ICRC Basic Emergency Care: Electrical injuries
IFRC First Aid Guidelines 2020 – Electrical injuries

description: Contact with electricity above 1000V, causing deep tissue damage, internal burns, cardiac arrest, and traumatic injuries from muscle contractions or falls.
causes: Contact with power lines or transformers
risk_factors: Working at height near electrical cables
Handling metal tools near overhead lines
Wet clothing or sweat increasing conductivity

common: Deep burns at entry and exit points

first_aid_steps: Ensure the power source is disconnected by professionals.
Do not approach within 10 meters of high-voltage lines until confirmed safe.
Check airway, breathing, and pulse immediately.
If no breathing, begin CPR and call emergency services.
Cover burns with sterile dressings without applying pressure.
Keep the person warm and monitor until help arrives.
what_not_to_do: Do not attempt rescue if the area is still energized.
Do not move the person unless necessary for safety.
Do not remove stuck clothing from burns.
Do not apply water to deep burns.
when_to_call_emergency: Any high-voltage exposure—always treated as an emergency.
Unconsciousness, breathing problems, or chest pain.
Severe burns or visible charring.
prevention: Strict safety protocols in industrial and construction sites.
Use insulated tools and gloves.
Maintain safe distance from live power lines.
references: WHO–ICRC Basic Emergency Care: Electrical injuries
IFRC First Aid Guidelines 2020 – Major trauma and burns

description: Direct or indirect exposure to lightning electrical discharge causing cardiac arrest, burns, shockwave trauma, and nervous system injury.
causes: Standing under trees or metal structures
Using wired electronics during a storm
first_aid_steps: Ensure scene safety—lightning can strike again.
Check breathing and pulse immediately.
Begin CPR if needed—lightning victims have the highest CPR survival rates.
Treat burns with sterile dressings.
Stabilize the spine if fall or blast injury is suspected.
Keep the person warm and reassure them.
what_not_to_do: Do not delay CPR—victims often recover if resuscitated fast.
Do not assume they are dead—brief cardiac arrest is common.
Do not move the person if there are signs of spinal injury.
when_to_call_emergency: Always — lightning injuries are medical emergencies.
Any unconsciousness or breathing difficulty.
Visible burns or trauma.
prevention: Avoid open spaces, beaches, and hilltops during storms.
Stay inside buildings or cars.
Do not use wired appliances during lightning storms.
references: WHO–ICRC Basic Emergency Care: Trauma assessment
IFRC First Aid Guidelines 2020 – Lightning injuries

description: Burn caused by electrical current passing through tissue, often deeper than surface burns and associated with heart rhythm disturbances.
causes: Damaged chargers or phones plugged into mains
first_aid_steps: Move the person only once the power is off.
Assess airway, breathing, and pulse.
Cool superficial burns with running water for 20 minutes.
Cover burns with clean, sterile dressing.
Monitor for heart rhythm changes or chest pain.
Seek medical evaluation even for small burns—internal damage may be severe.
what_not_to_do: Do not apply creams, oils, or toothpaste.
Do not break blisters.
Do not assume small surface burns mean minor injury.
when_to_call_emergency: Chest pain or palpitations after shock.
Loss of consciousness.
Burns involving face, hands, or genitals.
Any electrical injury in children.
prevention: Replace damaged sockets and water heaters.
Avoid using electrical devices near water.
Install proper grounding in homes.
references: WHO BEC: Electrical injuries
IFRC 2020: Burns and electrical emergencies

condition_name: Thermal burns (hot water, flame, hot surfaces)
description: Injury to skin from heat exposure. Severe burns can cause shock, infection, and disability.

danger_signs: Burns on face, hands, feet, or genitals

first_aid_steps: Cool the burned area under running cool water for 20 minutes.
Remove jewelry and tight clothing before swelling increases.
Cover burn with clean, non-stick dressing.
Keep patient warm to prevent hypothermia.
For large burns, lay flat and monitor for shock.
what_not_to_do: Do not use ice directly.
Do not apply toothpaste, butter, or oils.
Do not break blisters.
Do not remove stuck clothing.
when_to_call_emergency: Burns on face, hands, feet, or genitals.
Burns larger than the size of the patient’s palm.
Difficulty breathing, coughing soot.
Electrical or chemical burns.
prevention: Safe handling of hot liquids.
Fire safety in kitchens.
Childproofing homes.
references: WHO BEC – Burns
IFRC First Aid – Burn Management

description: A fracture where the bone communicates with the external environment through a break in the skin. High risk for infection, neurovascular injury, severe bleeding, and compartment syndrome. Requires immediate protection, immobilization, and urgent surgical management.
causes: Direct trauma with high kinetic energy

danger_signs: Severe swelling with increasing pain (compartment syndrome)

first_aid_steps: Control bleeding using pressure AROUND the wound; avoid pressing directly on exposed bone.
Cover the wound with sterile moist dressing or clean cloth if sterile materials unavailable.
Do NOT attempt to realign the bone.
Immobilize with splints above and below the fracture.
Check distal circulation, movement, sensation regularly.
Keep patient warm and treat for shock.
Urgent transfer to a surgical-capable hospital; requires IV antibiotics and operative debridement.
what_not_to_do: Do not push bone ends back inside.
Do not remove deeply embedded objects.
Do not irrigate vigorously in the field.
Do not allow patient to walk on limb.
Do not give anything orally.
when_to_call_emergency: Any open fracture regardless of size.
Loss of pulses or sensation in the limb.
Persistent bleeding despite pressure.
Multiple injuries (polytrauma).
prevention: Use of protective equipment at workplaces.
Fall prevention at homes and construction sites.
Safe machinery handling.
references: WHO BEC – Limb Trauma
ATLS 10th Edition – Open Fractures
Orthopaedic Trauma Association Guidelines

condition_name: Closed fracture (suspected bone break without open wound)
description: A break in the bone without skin penetration. Can cause significant internal bleeding, compartment syndrome, or neurovascular compromise. Requires immobilization and diagnostic imaging.

common: Difficulty or inability to move the limb
danger_signs: Severe pain unrelieved by immobilization (compartment syndrome)
Shortening or rotation of limb (displaced fracture)

first_aid_steps: Immobilize limb using splints above and below the fracture site.
Apply a padded soft dressing to prevent further injury.
Use cold compress wrapped in cloth for 20 minutes to reduce swelling.
Elevate limb if possible unless it worsens pain.
Monitor circulation, sensation, movement frequently.
Transport to medical facility for X-ray and orthopedic care.
what_not_to_do: Do not attempt to straighten the limb.
Do not apply ice directly to skin.
Do not let patient move or bear weight on injured limb.
Do not massage or manipulate fracture site.
when_to_call_emergency: Deformity with severe pain.
Absent pulse or numbness.
Severe swelling and tightness (suspected compartment syndrome).
prevention: Bone-strengthening diet and exercise.
Protective sports gear.
Fall-proof environments for elderly.
references: WHO BEC – Injuries
IFRC 2020 – Fracture Management
ATLS – Orthopedic Trauma

condition_name: Head trauma with danger signs (suspected brain injury)
description: Traumatic impact to the head causing potential intracranial bleeding, contusion, or diffuse brain injury. Danger signs require immediate evaluation due to risk of rapid deterioration.

danger_signs: Clear fluid from nose or ears (CSF leak)

first_aid_steps: Ensure cervical spine protection; keep patient still.
Lay patient on side if vomiting to protect airway.
Control scalp bleeding with gentle pressure.
Monitor airway, breathing, circulation continuously.
Check pupils, limb movement, and level of consciousness frequently.
Arrange urgent transfer to trauma center for CT scan.
what_not_to_do: Do not shake or move the patient abruptly.
Do not give anything orally.
Do not remove penetrating objects.
Do not allow patient to sleep if deteriorating.
when_to_call_emergency: Any loss of consciousness.
Vomiting more than once.
Seizures.
Weakness, confusion, or unequal pupils.
High-energy trauma mechanism.
prevention: Helmet use.
Safe sports practices.
Fall prevention.
Avoid alcohol while driving.
references: WHO BEC – Head Injury
ATLS – Head Trauma
IFRC 2020 – Head Injury First Aid

condition_name: Thermal burns (hot liquids, flame, hot surfaces)
description: Skin and tissue injury caused by heat exposure. Severity depends on depth, surface area, and body region. Risk of shock, infection, airway compromise, and disability.

danger_signs: Burns on face, neck → airway risk
Circumferential limb burns (risk of compartment syndrome)

first_aid_steps: Stop burning process immediately (remove from heat source).
Cool the burn with cool running water for 20 minutes; this reduces depth of burn.
Remove jewelry and tight clothing early.
Cover burn with sterile, non-adherent dressing.
Keep patient warm to prevent hypothermia.
If inhalation injury suspected: sit upright, provide high-flow oxygen if available.
Transport to burn-capable facility for severe burns.
what_not_to_do: Do not apply ice directly (causes vasoconstriction).
Do not use toothpaste, butter, oil, or traditional remedies.
Do not break blisters.
Do not remove clothing stuck to the burn.
when_to_call_emergency: Burns on face, hands, feet, genitals, or joints.
Burns > the size of the patient’s palm.
Electrical/chemical burns.
Signs of airway burn (soot, stridor).
prevention: Safe handling of hot liquids in kitchen.
Child-proofing hot-water areas.
Proper cylinder/gas storage.
Use of flame-retardant clothing in industry.
references: WHO Burn Management Guidelines
IFRC 2020 – Burns
American Burn Association Emergency Care Guidelines

description: Life-threatening chest injury where air enters the pleural space and cannot escape, causing lung collapse and shifting of the mediastinum. Rapidly fatal without immediate decompression.
causes: Blunt chest trauma with lung laceration

danger_signs: Absent breath sounds on one side
Tracheal deviation away from affected side

first_aid_steps: Provide high-flow oxygen if available.
Keep the patient sitting upright unless in shock.
Recognize classic triad: respiratory distress + absent breath sounds + hypotension.
Arrange immediate transport — this is a surgical emergency.
what_not_to_do: Do not delay transfer for diagnostic imaging.
Do not lay the patient flat unless in profound shock.
when_to_call_emergency: Any suspicion of tension pneumothorax.
Severe respiratory distress after chest trauma.
references: ATLS 10th Edition – Thoracic Trauma
WHO Basic Emergency Care – Chest Injuries

description: Air enters the pleural space through an open chest wound causing lung collapse. Characteristic ‘sucking’ sound with each breath. Fatal if not sealed quickly.

danger_signs: Decreased breath sounds on affected side

first_aid_steps: Cover the wound with an occlusive dressing taped on 3 sides to create a one-way valve.
If an object is embedded, do NOT remove it — secure it in place.
Provide oxygen if available.
Transport urgently to trauma care.
what_not_to_do: Do not completely seal the wound on all 4 sides (may cause tension pneumothorax).
Do not remove impaled objects.
when_to_call_emergency: All penetrating chest wounds.
Any sucking chest wound.
references: ATLS – Penetrating Chest Trauma
WHO Emergency Care Guidelines

description: Two or more adjacent ribs fractured in two places, producing a floating chest segment. Causes paradoxical chest movement and respiratory failure.
first_aid_steps: Provide oxygen if available.
Place the patient in semi-sitting position unless shocked.
Stabilize flail segment with bulky dressing or folded cloth.
Transport urgently to trauma center.
what_not_to_do: Do not bind the chest tightly.
Do not delay evacuation.
when_to_call_emergency: Any paradoxical chest movement.
Severe respiratory distress.
references: ATLS – Chest Wall Injury
WHO BEC – Chest Trauma

description: High-energy trauma causing pelvic ring disruption, leading to massive life-threatening internal hemorrhage.

common: Severe pelvic or lower abdominal pain

first_aid_steps: Apply pelvic binder or wrap tightly using a bedsheet around pelvic area.
Lay patient flat.
Treat for shock (warmth, no oral fluids).
Urgent transfer to trauma center.
what_not_to_do: Do not repeatedly press pelvis to check stability.
Do not allow patient to stand or move.
when_to_call_emergency: Any suspected pelvic fracture.
Signs of shock with no external bleeding.
references: ATLS – Pelvic Trauma
WHO Trauma Guidelines

condition_name: Blunt abdominal trauma with suspected internal bleeding
description: Traumatic impact to the abdomen risking damage to spleen, liver, or internal organs. Bleeding may be hidden and rapidly fatal.
first_aid_steps: Lay patient flat.
Treat for shock.
Do not give anything orally.
Urgent transport for imaging/surgery.
what_not_to_do: Do not apply pressure to abdomen.
Do not give oral medication or food.
when_to_call_emergency: Suspected internal bleeding.
Abdominal pain after high-energy trauma.
references: ATLS – Abdominal Trauma
WHO BEC Abdominal Injury

description: Injury caused by sharp objects entering the body. High risk of organ laceration, bleeding, and infection. Severity depends on trajectory and depth.
first_aid_steps: Control bleeding with pressure around wound.
If object is embedded, leave in place and stabilize.
Cover wound with sterile dressing.
Treat for shock.
Urgent evacuation to trauma center.
what_not_to_do: Do not pull out embedded objects.
Do not probe inside the wound.
when_to_call_emergency: Any penetrating wound to chest, abdomen, neck.
references: ATLS – Penetrating Trauma

description: Increased pressure within muscle compartments leading to ischemia and potential limb loss. Occurs after fractures, crush injuries, or burns.
first_aid_steps: Loosen constrictive dressings.
Keep the limb at heart level.
Urgent transport for surgical fasciotomy.
what_not_to_do: Do not elevate limb too high (reduces perfusion).
Do not apply ice.
when_to_call_emergency: Any suspected compartment syndrome.
references: Orthopaedic Trauma Association
ATLS – Extremity Trauma

description: Prolonged compression of muscles leading to muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis), hyperkalemia, kidney failure, and shock.
first_aid_steps: Remove crushing object carefully only if safe.
Start fluid therapy if available.
Monitor for shock.
Urgent transfer for laboratory evaluation and treatment.
what_not_to_do: Do not release a heavy crush suddenly (reperfusion shock).
Do not allow dehydration.
when_to_call_emergency: Any crush injury lasting >30 minutes.
Crush with collapse or dark urine.
references: WHO – Crush Syndrome Guidelines
ATLS – Special Trauma Situations
